content:
A missed deadline usually means that particular competition is closed. Check the official instructions before doing anything else, then look for later rounds, separate awards or the next intake.

The 2026-27 funding calendar, mapped

Major European schemes cluster their deadlines so a missed window almost always has a successor. DAAD research grants close mainly between August and October for the following year; RISE Germany runs mid-October to early December for the next summer; Erasmus Mundus programmes open October-January for the following September; MSCA Doctoral Networks publish vacancies in bursts tied to call deadlines — the current call closes 24 November 2026; country awards (Chevening, Commonwealth, Holland Scholarship) each hold their own windows. The chart maps the months; the real skill is reading each scheme's page, because calls move year to year.

Two always-open routes exist alongside the calendar. University-specific and departmental funding — fee waivers, completion grants, emergency funds — accepts applications year-round. And doctoral vacancies with employment contracts (German E13 positions, Dutch cao NU positions, Nordic salaried PhDs) are advertised continuously on EURAXESS and university job boards with their own closing dates, so a missed scholarship deadline costs you one route out of several, not the year.

[[chart:deadline-calendar]][[chart:always-open]]

Turning a missed round into the next one

The useful move after a missed deadline is a calendar reversal, not regret. Take the scheme's next cycle and place your milestones backwards: host contact three to eight weeks before submission, references six weeks out, transcripts and translations a month ahead, and the application itself drafted three weeks early so the final week is verification rather than writing. For DAAD that means the host search starts in spring for an autumn deadline; for Erasmus Mundus, the shortlist of programmes is built in September for October-January windows; for MSCA, watch EURAXESS from the call's opening, because vacancies appear in waves and the best ones close early.

Meanwhile the year is not empty. Salaried vacancies and rolling university grants run continuously, and they reward exactly the documents the next scholarship round needs: a focused CV, a research statement and a reference packet that can be sent within a week. Treat every rolling application this year as a rehearsal that also pays — the applicant who has submitted five rolling applications by January walks into the next deadline cycle with sharper materials than someone who waited for the calendar.

Check whether the deadline has really passed

Read the official deadline, time zone and submission instructions. An application portal remaining accessible does not necessarily mean late applications are accepted. If a published instruction permits late submissions, follow it; otherwise, ask the admissions or scholarship office one concise question before investing more time.

Separate admission from funding

A course may still accept applications after its scholarship competition closes. Check both deadlines and make sure an admission offer would be financially workable. Consider another funding round, a different intake or a funded project with a later deadline rather than assuming an unfunded offer will gain support.

Prepare for the next round

Record the next announced opening date, request references early and review the criteria you previously missed. Keep reusable documents ready, but update each statement for the new programme. Continue applying to suitable live opportunities while you wait.

Use the missed round to improve the next application

Write down what was ready before the deadline and what was still missing. If references were late, request them earlier next time. If the statement took too long, create an evidence outline that you can adapt without sending the same generic text everywhere. Keep a calendar for the next announced round and continue checking other suitable awards. If you contact the funding office, ask one factual question about late submissions or later rounds. Do not claim a technical problem or exceptional circumstance unless it actually happened.

Establish which deadline you missed

First check the date, time zone and application stage in the official announcement. A university admission deadline, scholarship deadline, departmental nomination and reference deadline can be separate. If an application portal remains open, that does not necessarily mean the scholarship competition is still accepting submissions.

Retain the announcement and any relevant confirmation. If there appears to be a technical issue or contradictory information, contact the named office promptly with a concise description and evidence. Do not alter a screenshot or claim that a system failed when you simply missed the date.

Five useful options to investigate

OptionWhat to verify before acting
Ask the official contactWhether any published late-submission process applies to your circumstances.
Check later roundsWhether another round actually exists and who is eligible.
Separate admission and fundingWhether an academic application remains open without implying an award.
Search other awardsEligibility, real deadlines and the costs each award covers.
Prepare for the next intakeWhether the scheme is expected to reopen and what is officially confirmed.

These are routes to investigate, not five guaranteed ways to recover a missed award. If the funder says the competition is closed with no exception, use that answer to plan the next step. Repeated emails do not create a late-submission route.

A concise enquiry about the closed round

"I intended to apply for [award/intake] and have seen that the published deadline was [date/time zone]. Could you confirm whether applications are now closed and whether any formal late-submission or later-round process applies? I understand if the deadline is final."

Use a more specific message if you have a genuine documented issue. Include the application reference where one exists and keep personal information proportionate to the question. Ask for the applicable process rather than requesting an informal exception from someone who may not have authority to grant one.

Do not replace a scholarship with an unplanned debt

If admission remains available, ask whether the place is funded, partly funded or self-funded. Calculate the resulting fees and living costs before accepting. The fact that you can still enrol does not establish that the original financial plan remains workable. Check deposit and withdrawal terms before making a payment.

For another scholarship, read the whole announcement rather than choosing the nearest deadline. A later award may support a different subject, applicant group or period. Keep possible support separate from funding already awarded, and check whether the university must nominate you before a separate earlier date.

Make the next round easier to submit

Identify why the deadline was missed in practical terms: an unknown nomination date, missing document, delayed reference or insufficient time to draft. Choose a corrective step for that issue. Set internal dates for tasks you control and earlier requests for tasks requiring someone else. Save accurate material you can reuse, while checking the next cycle's actual prompt and conditions.

Will a professor be able to extend the scholarship deadline?

Only the relevant process can establish who has that authority. Ask the named scholarship office or contact rather than assuming supervisor support creates an exception.

Should I submit anyway if the portal allows it?

Check the official instructions. An open portal can serve other courses or rounds. Ask whether the submission would be considered for the award before relying on it.

Check whether a deferral changes funding

If the university permits you to defer admission, ask whether any scholarship application or award carries forward. Do not assume academic and funding deferrals are the same decision. The next intake may have a different competition, eligibility date or award amount. Record the answer and any conditions before accepting a deferred place. If a new application is required, use the extra time to improve the evidence that matters to the criteria. Keep existing references and documents available, but check whether the next cycle needs updated versions. A deferral is useful only when the revised timeline and financial plan are both clear enough for you to act on.

Check whether a new round requires new referee submissions rather than assuming the earlier references transfer automatically.

Questions applicants often ask

Can I still get funding if scholarship deadlines have passed?

Usually yes, through three routes: salaried doctoral vacancies advertised year-round on EURAXESS and university boards; university-specific grants with rolling windows; and the next round of most schemes, which repeats annually. One missed deadline rarely closes the whole year.

When do DAAD and Erasmus Mundus deadlines fall?

DAAD research grants typically close August-October; RISE Germany ran 15 October to 30 November 2026 for summer 2027. Erasmus Mundus programmes accept applications roughly October to January for the following September intake.

Requirements and policies should be checked for your programme and application date.
